title: How far is the laddu on a long edge of the box?
description: A cuboid is eight centimetres by four centimetres by four centimetres, with an ant at the centre of an end face and a laddu on a long bottom edge. The board unfolds the end face against the long face and finds the slanted line with the right triangle rule. Keeko's doubt is that the path is six centimetres.
teaching_notes: One idea: unfold the end face against the long face, then the shortest path is a slanted straight line whose length comes from a right triangle. Watch for students who walk along the edges and add the pieces.

video_script.why: The child finds the shortest path on a box by unfolding the end face against the long face and using the right triangle rule, because the straight line on the flat sheet is slanted.
video_script.substitution: cuboid 8 cm by 4 cm by 4 cm; end face unfolded against the long face; ant 2 cm from the fold and 2 cm above the bottom edge line; laddu 2 cm beyond the fold on the line; 2 + 2 = 4 along and 2 across; path = square root of (4 x 4 + 2 x 2) = square root of 20, about 4.47 cm.
video_script.anchor: the box of the book with the ant on the end face and the laddu on the long bottom edge, the end face unfolded against the long face
video_script.wrong_answer: the ant walks two down, two across and two along, so the path is six centimetres
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko adds the pieces of a bent path along the edges, 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 cm; on the flat net a straight line joins the ant to the laddu and is shorter, about 4.47 cm, so the doubt is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: The shortest path is about four point four seven centimetres, a slanted straight line

final_answer.value: About 4.47 cm, a slanted straight line on the net
final_answer.spoken: about four point four seven centimetres, a slanted straight line on the net

hold_back: About 4.47 cm, a slanted straight line on the net
maths_rules: a path on the box and the matching path on the net have the same length
unfold the end face flat against the long face that meets the laddu's edge
on the net the ant is 2 cm from the fold and 2 cm above the bottom edge line; the laddu is 2 cm beyond the fold, on that line
right triangle with sides 4 and 2: path squared = 4 x 4 + 2 x 2 = 16 + 4 = 20
path = square root of 20, about 4.47 cm
wrong idea: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 cm is a bent path along the edges and is longer than the straight line
video_script.design: One idea: unfold, draw the slanted line, and use the right triangle. The end face swings flat against the long face; the slanted line is drawn in the accent colour and the bent route in the warning colour.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about an ant and a laddu on a box.
<bookmark mark='box'/>The box is eight centimetres long, with an end face of four centimetres by four centimetres.
<bookmark mark='ant'/>The ant is at the centre of the end face.
<bookmark mark='laddu'/>The laddu sits on a long bottom edge, two centimetres from that end.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>The ant can walk only on the surface. Find the shortest path.

narration: <bookmark mark='along'/>Step two, measure the gap. The ant is two centimetres from the fold, and the laddu is two centimetres beyond it. That is four centimetres along.
<bookmark mark='across'/>The ant is two centimetres above the bottom edge line, and the laddu is on that line. That is two centimetres across.

narration: <bookmark mark='tri'/>Step three, the straight line is the longest side of a right triangle with sides four and two.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>The {{NAME_1}} Theorem applies to a right triangle. It says the square of the longest side is the sum of the squares of the other two.
<bookmark mark='work'/>Four times four is sixteen, and two times two is four. Sixteen plus four is twenty. The path is the square root of twenty.
